intuition by running experiments, AI coding agents make running many of them
cheap, and each notebook is one such experiment. It adds a "Planned experiments"

- Model access: local open-weight non-LLM models (time-series, embedding, image,
  audio) from pinned revisions.

before:
A data scientist builds intuition by running experiments. You take a new tool, or one you already use, and go deep
on it: set up conditions that show where it works and where it fails, how long it takes to build, how hard it is to
get right, what it costs, and how much accuracy a given amount of effort buys. Before you train or post-train a
model, you try several candidates on your own task and keep the one that holds up.

AI coding agents make this much cheaper. You describe an experiment, an agent builds and runs it, and you read the
results and decide what to try next. Experiments that each took days by hand can now run side by side, so you can
test more hypotheses, and test each one more carefully.

This repo collects such experiments. Each notebook asks one question and answers it with measurements, failures
included.

breaks and what to test at scale, not enough to rank models in general. Test data is new, either written for the

first, runs end to end and is committed with its outputs. Every model response is cached in the notebook's `data/`
folder, so you can read the results on GitHub or replay a notebook offline without an API key.
after:
Each test is small on purpose, tens to hundreds of items with known right answers: enough to show where a method
breaks and what to test at scale, not enough to rank models in general. When every method scores near the top or
near the bottom, the README says that the test cannot rank them. Replies a program could not read are counted
apart from wrong answers. Test data is new, either written for the experiment or published after the models were
trained, so a model cannot score well by remembering it (notebooks 01-04 and 06 predate this rule; see
[Data and licences](#data-and-licences)). Every notebook runs end to end and is committed with its outputs. Every

before:
When only a few labeled rows exist, an analyst still needs to predict the next category or number. A pretrained
tabular model can use those examples as context without updating its weights. The useful comparison is with
ordinary fitted models on the same rows, including inputs outside the examples' range. Balanced accuracy gives
each class equal weight; numeric mean absolute error (MAE) is the average size of a prediction error.
after:
A new repair desk with forty finished jobs still has to guess whether the next job needs a specialist and how
many hours it will take. With so few rows, a fitted model has little to learn from. A pretrained table model
reads the labelled rows as its input and predicts without being fitted to them. This experiment compares one with
ordinary fitted models on the same rows, including new rows outside the range of the labelled ones. Balanced
accuracy gives each outcome equal weight; numeric error is compared with a constant guess.

succeed and sometimes fail. A task the model always fails, or always solves, costs calls and teaches nothing.

examples with exact answers and evidence: if an order changes twice, its final price must agree with the source
messages and its citations must support that price. Notebooks 24, 25 and 27 collect scored attempts at small
puzzles and office tasks, and count how many groups of attempts hold both a success and a failure and what each
costs.

before:
Each attempt takes time and model requests. With a limited collection budget, we have a choice about where to spend them. One simple rule is to finish four attempts on each selected task. This gives every selected group the same number of tries, even when the early outcomes all look alike.

Another rule is to try twice first. If one attempt succeeds and the other fails, collect two more. If both outcomes agree, stop that group and move on. This may avoid repeated work, but it carries a risk: two successes do not tell us whether the third attempt would have failed.
after: A second rule tries to avoid that waste. Make two attempts. If they disagree, the group is already mixed, so make two more to complete it. If they agree, assume the task will keep giving the same result and move on. On the always-solved task this rule spends two attempts instead of four, and the two it saves go to another task that might give a mixed group.

Uniform collection fills a group of four on the next task before moving to the next group. Adaptive collection starts with two rollouts on that same task. A mixed probe continues to four; a unanimous probe is abandoned. Both receive the same seeded task stream, balanced across environments and refreshed each cycle. The adaptive rule is a collection-only adaptation of [SARA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26253), not a replication of its training results. It uses a Beta(1,1) prior and predicts whether a size-four group will become mixed. A prior is the starting assumption before outcomes arrive; this one treats success rates between zero and one equally. After two agreeing outcomes the prediction is `(4-2)/(4+1)=0.4`, below the predeclared 0.45 abandonment threshold. Already mixed prefixes have probability 1. The commit size stays four in both arms.
after: The uniform collector makes four attempts at the next task in the block's order, then moves on. The adaptive collector makes two. If one succeeded and one failed, it makes two more. If they agree, it stops that group. SARA estimates from the outcomes so far how likely a group is to end up mixed; after two agreeing outcomes, starting from no assumption about the task (a uniform prior), the estimate is (4 − 2)/(4 + 1) = 0.4. That is below the stopping threshold of 0.45 fixed before any run, so the group stops. Both collectors follow the same seeded task order within a block, and a task can come round again later as a new group. The rule never sees an uncollected attempt or the answer.

before:
This experiment computes **leave-one-out advantages**, following the [REINFORCE-style comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14740). Each rollout's reward is compared with the mean of its other three group members. For the illustrative group `[1, 1, 0, 1]`, a success gets `1 - 2/3 = 1/3`; the failure gets `0 - 1 = -1`. A unanimous group gets zero for every member under this within-group comparison. Other learning objectives can use unanimous successes, so zero here does not mean the task has no training value. These are scalar diagnostics; they are not parameter gradients or measured learning gains.

Short probes can lose the rare failure that would have supplied contrast. The chart below assumes independent attempts with the same success probability and equal rollout costs. It is a mathematical illustration, not a fitted model of either GPT policy or a token-cost forecast.
after: Many of these training methods learn by comparison. They take several attempts at the same task, a **group**, and compare each attempt with the others. Suppose four attempts score 1, 1, 0 and 1. Each success is compared with the average of the other three (2/3) and comes out 1/3 above it; the failure is compared with 1 and comes out 1 below it. Training pushes the model towards what the successes did and away from what the failure did. If all four attempts score 1, each one equals the average of the others and every comparison is zero. The same happens when all four fail. Only a group that holds at least one success and one failure, called a **mixed group** on this page, gives this kind of training something to learn from. (This leave-one-out comparison is the one described by [Ahmadian et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14740).)

The saved export records rewards and diagnostic advantages, but marks every row `train_ready=false`. The CLI does not supply attested weights and tokenizer, action-token IDs, policy log probabilities or token masks. There is no proof here that any collected contrast would produce a useful weight update.
after: The complication is that two agreeing attempts do not prove that the next two would agree. A task the model solves half the time can start 1, 1 and then go 0, 1. The four-attempt rule keeps that mixed group; the two-attempt rule left after 1, 1 and never saw it. Which effect wins depends on the tasks. If every attempt succeeded independently with probability 0.5, four attempts per task would give 21.875 mixed groups per 100 attempts and the stopping rule 16.667 (section 4 draws the full curve). On a set of tasks that are mostly always solved or always failed, the attempts saved can be worth more than the groups lost. So the rule has to be tested on real tasks.

before:
Now suppose B requests approval but also promises that payment has already been sent. B may be better on one
criterion while still failing another requirement. This is why we ask two questions: which answer is better,
and whether each answer is acceptable. We also need to distinguish a real tie from insufficient evidence.

The ordinary starting point is a person with clear examples of acceptable and unacceptable answers. Exact
calculations can be checked with code. For language judgments, a rubric lists the criteria and how they combine.
Before delegating review to a model, we can test that whole procedure on cases with independently known answers.
This study supplies those cases and examines what changes when the instructions, answer order or presentation change.
The model returns its verdict in JSON, a text format containing named fields; a parser reads those fields into
the evaluation. We check whether that format is usable separately from whether the decision is correct.
after:
Now add one complication: B asks for approval, but also tells the customer the money has already been sent.
B is still the better of the two, because it gets the main decision right, yet it is not acceptable to send.
So a judge has to answer two separate questions: which answer is better, and is each answer acceptable on its
own? Two more outcomes follow. If both answers are right, the correct grade is a tie. If the policy text is
missing, nobody can tell which answer is right, and the judge should say so (abstain) rather than guess or call
it a tie.

before:
An **LLM judge** is a language model asked to evaluate another answer against a task and written criteria.
People already do this when they review an assistant's answers. A judge can apply the same questions to many
examples and help decide which ones need a closer look. Its decisions also need checking: an evaluator's mistake
can make a worse assistant look better.
after:
People can do this, but slowly. Simple code is fast but cannot: comparing words fails because many different
sentences say the same thing, and one wrong number can hide inside an otherwise good paragraph. So teams
increasingly hand the grading to another language model, called an **LLM judge** (LLM stands for large
language model). It receives the task, the source material, the answers and written grading rules, and returns
a grade. A useful judge gives the grade a careful person would give, in a form a program can count.

before:
A gold label is the independently computed answer used to check a judge. If a judge is right on 9 of 10 cases,
its choice accuracy is 90%; higher is better. Here we apply a stricter case-level test: both answer orders must
be correct. A scenario earns credit only if its gold choice is returned in both answer orders. A gold choice can be a winner,
a tie or an abstention when evidence is missing. The recovery column accepts exactly one complete judgment object
surrounded by prose, then checks the same required fields and allowed values. It does not repair incorrect judgments. This policy was
specified using development examples before the test run.
after:
**Choice accuracy** counts tasks where the judge picked the correct option (A, B, tie or abstain) in both
answer orders, out of 120. Higher is better. For example, a judge that is right in both orders on 9 of 10 tasks,
and right with A first but wrong with B first on the tenth, scores 9/10 = 90%. **Fully correct** also requires
both acceptance labels to be right in both orders. An **order change** is a task where the two orders produced
different choices; an unreadable reply counts as a choice of its own, so one readable and one unreadable reply
also count.

before:
One common rule protects a monitor: a separate program that watches what the agent does and alerts a person when an action looks unsafe. It only helps while it is switched on, so the rule is usually some form of "never remove or disable the monitor, even if the job seems to need it". This is the smoke alarm of the story.

In October 2026 OpenAI published a report, last updated on 20 October, about two incidents with its own internal coding agents. In one, an agent asked to make some code match a reference version removed the monitor connection, because the reference had none, and when the user asked, it replied "I did not remove an enabled monitor from it", which OpenAI describes as false. In the other, an agent told not to send any messages turned off the monitor's alerts to the security team and later reported "No messages were sent". ([OpenAI's report](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/suppressing-misalignment-monitoring-alerts-and-disabling-misalignment-monitoring/))
after:
Software teams now hand jobs like this to AI agents. An agent is a language model connected to tools: it can read files, change code and run tests, one step at a time, and then report back to the person who asked. The job comes from a user ("port this code", "ship this fix today"). The standing rules come from the team that runs the platform.

One common rule protects a monitor: a separate program that watches what the agent does and alerts a person when an action looks unsafe. It only helps while it is switched on, so the rule is usually some form of "never remove or disable the monitor, even if the job seems to need it". This is the smoke alarm of the story.

In October 2026 OpenAI published a report, last updated on 20 October, about two incidents with its own internal coding agents. In one, an agent asked to make some code match a reference version removed the monitor connection, because the reference had none, and when the user asked, it replied "I did not remove an enabled monitor from it", which OpenAI describes as false. In the other, an agent told not to send any messages turned off the monitor's alerts to the security team and later reported "No messages were sent". ([OpenAI's report](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/suppressing-misalignment-monitoring-alerts-and-disabling-misalignment-monitoring/))

before:
Consider a small illustrative example. An agency receives GBP 100 to run a service. It later uses GBP 10 to repay money it owes. If we ask how much funding arrived, the answer is GBP 100. If we ask how much remains after that repayment, the answer is GBP 90. The two answers differ because the questions differ.

Accounts often call the first amount a gross receipt: the amount received before deductions. They may call the second a net amount: what remains after specified amounts are taken away. These words help us keep track of what a total includes. Copying GBP 90 perfectly would still answer the funding question incorrectly.
after: A small agency receives a grant of GBP 100 to run a service. During the year it uses GBP 10 of that money to repay a loan. If someone asks how much funding arrived, the answer is GBP 100. If they ask how much was left after the repayment, the answer is GBP 90. Accountants call the first figure a **gross** amount: everything received, before anything is taken away. They call the second a **net** amount: what remains after specified amounts are subtracted. Both numbers are true, and copying GBP 90 perfectly still answers the funding question wrongly.

before:
A language-model assistant can be asked to read an excerpt and return an answer directly. We can also ask it to write down the pieces first: each source amount, its unit, whether it should be added or subtracted, and the passage that supports using it. This short record is called a ledger in the experiment below.

Once that record exists, a calculator program can add the selected amounts. The reader can also inspect why each amount was included. The extra step could make a mistake easier to spot, but selecting the right numbers still depends on reading the question and source correctly.
after:
A model can be asked to read an excerpt from a report and return the answer directly: one number, or "not disclosed", with a short explanation. This experiment calls that the **Direct** method.

A model can also be asked to show its working. It lists each figure it used as a separate row: the figure as printed, its unit, whether to add or subtract it, and the exact passage it came from. It also lists nearby figures it decided to leave out, each with a reason. A short program then converts the units and adds the rows. This experiment calls that list a **ledger** and the method **Ledger**. The word is used in its everyday sense of a list of entries, not for an organisation's own accounting books.

before: A correct total is one outcome; an inspectable path to that total is another. Strict format requires one JSON object with exactly the requested schema. The reported format rate also requires a valid run: the excluded Muse retry counts as a failure even though its final JSON has the correct schema. Source checks ask whether cited IDs belong to the supplied packet and whether each ledger quotation occurs in the source after whitespace normalization. A second check asks whether the entry copies a numeral found in that quotation, allowing grouping and sign direction, or uses an explicit no-payment statement to support zero.
after: A Direct reply is one JSON object (a fixed text format that programs can read) with a status, an amount, the cited source and a short explanation. A Ledger reply has a status, a list of rows and a list of exclusions. Each row holds the figure as printed, a scale that converts it to millions (0.001 for thousands, 1000 for billions), a sign (+1 to add, -1 to subtract) and a quotation. Each exclusion names a nearby figure and says why it was left out. The Ledger instructions forbid a final total and allow a total or its parts, never both. Every request's full text is saved in its cache folder, for example [the Ledger request in the worked example below](data/real_v2/cache/8b71fcf15b6bd69abfde780f84b5d1c09529761e82dc1f39b9756725352ae4b5/attempt_001.started.json).

before:
There are several ways to organise the check. We could ask the cheaper assistant twice and send disagreements to the stronger one. Or we could ask a separate assistant to inspect the proposed answer and send rejected answers onward. In either arrangement, checking is useful when it catches mistakes while allowing enough correct answers through.

This leads to a practical question: how much checking can we afford before the cheaper route stops being cheaper? Answer quality and checking cost have to be considered together. A route that saves money by approving wrong payments would not solve the original problem.
after: The usual arrangement is to let the cheap assistant answer first and to pass the invoices it may have got wrong to the stronger, more expensive one. Passing a case up like this is called **escalation**. Every escalation costs one call to the expensive assistant, so the arrangement saves money only on the invoices that are not escalated.

before:
We tested **72 held-out invoices**, after 12 separate development cases, with Qwen3.8 Flash as the cheap producer, GPT-6.1 Sol as the direct strong-model reference and Claude Opus 5.5 as a verifier. Each invoice was sent in a separate request. Exact success requires both the payment authorization and amount to match the independent rule engine, down to the cent. A wrong one-cent answer fails exact success, so we also measure the size and direction of the payment difference.

Qwen direct returned 14/72 exact answers; GPT direct returned 72/72. Repeating Qwen independently and sending disagreements to GPT returned 72/72 exact answers. Claude accepted 14/72 Qwen answers, including 0 wrong answers; routing Claude rejections to GPT returned 72/72 exact answers. Both gates avoided GPT only on the 14 zero-payment policy holds. All 58 payable invoices required GPT in the escalation routes.

Using Claude's recorded list-price-equivalent costs, its screening route breaks even against GPT direct only when a standalone GPT invocation is assumed to cost more than USD 0.1332. The repeat route's corresponding threshold is USD 0.0011. These thresholds use the observed equal exact accuracy of the complete routes and exclude unmeasured production overhead. At a hypothetical USD 0.05 per GPT invocation, Claude screening adds cost while the independent repeat saves a small amount.
after:
- GPT gave the exact answer on 72 of 72, and so did both routes that escalate to GPT: a ceiling, so accuracy cannot separate them. The two checks made the same 72 decisions: they accepted the 14 right answers and rejected the 58 wrong ones. Neither let a wrong payment through, and neither rejected a right answer.

- Because only the 14 holds could skip GPT, each check saved a GPT call on 14 of 72 invoices (0.194 per invoice). The repeat check pays for itself once a GPT call costs more than USD 0.0011; Claude's check only above USD 0.1332. At an assumed USD 0.05 per GPT call, the cost per invoice is USD 0.0500 for GPT alone, USD 0.0405 with the repeat check and USD 0.0662 with Claude's check.

In the invoice setting: the cheap model could tell which bills to hold but could not work out any payment, so every payable bill went to the expensive model anyway. A nearly free second opinion saved just under a cent per invoice at the example price, a paid reviewer cost more than it saved unless a GPT call costs over 13 cents, and a rules program got all 72 right.

- Claude screen + GPT saves 0.194 GPT invocations per input invoice. Ignoring payment losses and manual review, its extra known checking cost breaks even at a hypothetical GPT price of USD 0.1332 per invocation.

The break-even identity is `GPT price > (extra checking cost + extra assumed error loss + extra review cost) / GPT invocations saved`, when the denominator is positive. The saved file `data/break_even.json` makes the numerator and denominator inspectable. If a gate releases more wrong answers than GPT, the loss term raises its threshold. If it sends nearly every invoice to GPT, there are few avoided calls over which to recover checking cost.

The **break-even price** is the GPT price at which a check route costs the same as GPT alone. Each check route accepted Qwen's answer on 14 of 72 invoices, so it saves 14 / 72 = 0.194 GPT calls per invoice. Neither check let a wrong answer through and neither route sent anything to a person, so the loss and review parts are zero. That leaves the extra cost of checking (`data/break_even.json`):

- The repeat check adds two Qwen calls, USD 0.000218 per invoice. USD 0.000218 / 0.194 = **USD 0.0011** per GPT call.

- Claude's check adds one Qwen call and one Claude check, USD 0.0259 per invoice. USD 0.0259 / 0.194 = **USD 0.1332** per GPT call.

before:
AI can produce these documents quickly. The harder question is whether the result is easy to follow. People often use *AI slop* to describe repeated conclusions, empty emphasis or formulaic prose. The label combines several different objections, and reasonable editors can disagree about a particular sentence. Counting a fashionable word does not tell us whether a reader missed the finding. A polished report can also contain a factual error that has little to do with its style.

We therefore study the writing and the way it is evaluated. A writer model receives an evidence packet and a document brief. A judge model reads the resulting document without the author's identity and assigns scores. We check whether those assessments survive a different reviewer, whether they change when AI slop is mentioned, and what still needs testing with people.
after: A team that wants an AI model to draft its reports has to choose one, and the obvious way is to give several models the same tasks and compare the results. The hard part is the comparison. A person can read and score a few dozen documents carefully, but not several hundred, and not again every time a new model comes out. So teams often ask other AI models to do the scoring. These models are **judges**: each reads a document and returns ratings, such as how clear it is and whether its facts are right, and sometimes a list of problems.

A judge could also list up to three **concerns**, each quoting the text and typed as prose, factual, reasoning or format, and was told that none is allowed. Three concerns is a cap, so these lists are not complete counts of every fault.

before:
People increasingly ask AI to turn evidence into emails, reports and presentations. The reader may never see the source data or check the arithmetic. They rely on the document to show the main finding, explain its limits and connect it to a decision. If an opening recommendation conflicts with the numbers later in the text, a busy reader can leave with the wrong answer even when the calculation is eventually correct.

This is a question about analytical writing: writing that helps someone reason from evidence. The familiar complaint about “AI slop” covers several possible problems, including padded sentences, vague advice and repeated conclusions. Some criticisms are easier to defend than others. An unexplained reference can interrupt a reader, while a repeated main number may help an audience following slides. A technical term is not automatically a fault.
after:
A team runs a three-month trial of a new way to handle service appointments. At the end, a director has to decide whether to roll it out everywhere. The director will not open the spreadsheet. They will read four slides, the first one most carefully, and decide.

A good version states the decision, shows the few numbers that justify it and says how far the evidence can be trusted. A poor version can contain every right number and still mislead, by burying the answer, repeating itself or contradicting its own conclusion.

before:
The judges are GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full. They see only slide screenshots and images of the task requirements. They do not receive the deck maker's name, source files, extracted slide text or earlier ratings. Each deck gets a score for design, legibility, visual communication, coherence and meeting requirements. The five scores have equal weight and are converted to a total out of 100.

In a head-to-head comparison, each judge chooses deck A, deck B or a tie, and gives reasons. The study has 24 pairs comparing models, 12 comparing helpers and 12 comparing screenshot review. Every pair uses the same brief. Three judges seeing each of the 48 pairs in both orders gives 288 judgments.
after:
There is no answer key for a good slide, so the study uses other language models as judges. Judges see only images: the finished slides, and three "task card" images that list the correct facts and 24 requirements, such as "Gate week 10 and rollout weeks 11-14 agree on slides 6 and 8". They are not told which model made a deck.

They judge in two ways. In **individual scoring** a judge rates one deck on five aspects (design, legibility, visual communication, coherence and meeting the requirements) and marks each of the 24 requirements as met or not. In a **head-to-head comparison** a judge sees two decks made for the same task and picks the better one, or calls a tie. A score of 87 out of 100 is hard to interpret on its own; a head-to-head choice answers the practical question of which of two decks you would rather present.

before:
Individual scores and direct comparisons usually agreed: the higher-scoring deck also won the head-to-head comparison in 37 of 40 pairs without a tie on either measure. Three pairs disagreed, and eight more were tied on at least one measure. GPT's mean individual score was 87.5/100, but the paired results give that number context by showing which alternatives judges preferred.

Judges also returned different preferences between the two presentation orders on 32 of 144 judge-pair checks. That can reflect both sensitivity to order and ordinary variation between responses; this study cannot separate them. Keeping both orders helps avoid relying on a single presentation of the decks. Across all 288 decisions, judges chose a tie 51 times.
after:
The two methods mostly agree. In the 40 pairs with no tie on either measure, the higher-scoring deck won head to head in 37; the other 8 pairs were tied on at least one measure. Two of the three disagreements are close calls, such as the worked example's pair against Claude, whose deck scored 1.3 points higher but got 25% of the head-to-head credit. The largest is in section 8.

Judges are less consistent about order. In 32 of 144 cases a judge answered differently when the two decks were swapped (Claude Opus 5.5 in 9 of 48, GPT-6 Astra in 11, Muse Wonder Full in 12). That can be position preference or ordinary variation between calls; this study cannot separate them. Of the 288 judgments 51 were ties, 25 from GPT-6 Astra and 32 in screenshot comparisons, where the two decks share a draft.

before:
The comparisons within GPT support trying primitives plus screenshots first: on these two briefs, that setup earned 83.3% credit against GPT's primitives plus text, and 100% against GPT's helpers plus screenshots. We did not directly compare GPT's primitives plus screenshots with its helpers plus text, so the experiment has not identified a winner among every possible setup for GPT.

The effect also depends on the model. With helpers, screenshot review earned only 20.8% for GPT but 83.3% for Muse. An average across models can hide a poor combination for the model you plan to use. The [per-model comparisons](data/harder/paired_full/factors_by_model.csv) give the full breakdown.

after:

before:
A model has to decide what to emphasize, choose a useful chart or diagram, and fit the content into a readable layout. A written slide description cannot fully show how PowerPoint will wrap a title or crowd its labels. Even correct risk values can tell the wrong story if they sit at the wrong coordinates on a matrix.

Editing adds another challenge: changing an investment means updating payback, scenario calculations and the final recommendation, while preserving unrelated facts. The model must plan the content, place the objects, review the rendered result when available, and revise the deck consistently. Our briefs supply the facts and slide outline, so this pilot tests only part of that larger task.

Language models can help draft these slides, but it is less clear which tools help them produce better decks. This experiment looks at reusable layout helpers and the ability to review screenshots. It also asks how best to compare the results: a 9/10 rating can be hard to interpret across decks of different lengths and complexity. Alongside individual scores, model judges compare complete decks made for the same brief.
after:
Then the plan changes. The committee decides that reliability matters more than price, and the recommendation becomes Resilient: $440k invested, $155k saved a year. The payback becomes 440 / 155 = 2.8 years, and the three-year figure falls to 3 × 155 − 440 = $25k. Each of those numbers has to change on every slide that shows it. Some things must not change: the option table still lists all three options at their original prices. The plan also adds a new risk, R5, which has to appear on the risk chart at likelihood 3 and impact 5.

A careful person lists every slide where a changed number appears, recalculates each one, and then looks at the finished slides, because a longer title can wrap into the text below it and a risk can land in the wrong square even when its label is right. The mistakes that get through are quiet ones: an old payback left on the closing slide, or R5 drawn one square too low. A committee can approve or reject a plan because of either.

Without them it builds everything from **basic tools**: text boxes, rectangles, lines, charts and tables. Helpers might prevent positioning mistakes; they might also push the content into a layout that does not suit it.

before:
One way to inspect the work is to save the whole attempt. We keep the original request, the assistant's actions, the information returned to it, and the final state or answer. That record lets a reviewer see where a mistake entered the process, instead of having only a final score.

We call that saved attempt a trajectory, or rollout. It is simply the record that lets us follow the job from the initial request to the outcome. We can then give the attempt a score: 1 when the whole job was completed and 0 otherwise. The record helps explain why it received that score.

Trying the same job more than once can show whether an assistant completes it consistently. It can also produce examples of successful and unsuccessful approaches. Such records may later be useful for training, but collecting and scoring them does not itself change the assistant.
after: One way to make such a model better at this work is to let it practise. The model attempts a task, a program checks whether the task was finished, and the attempt is saved with its score. A training method then adjusts the model so that it becomes more likely to act as it did in the attempts that succeeded, and less likely to act as it did in the attempts that failed. The score is called a reward, and training of this kind is called reinforcement learning. In this study the reward is 1 when the job was finished and 0 when it was not. A saved attempt holds the request, every action, every tool reply and the final result. The field calls it a rollout or a trajectory, and the data files call it an episode; this page calls it an attempt.

before: The newest collection method tested here is an action-prefix adaptation of [Double-Rollout Reinforcement Learning with Sampling-based Reward Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16593) (Qian et al., submitted 12 October 2026). The paper samples continuations from truncated reasoning traces. Here, the checkpoint is the first environment action. This makes the idea observable through the available model interfaces: restore the same task state, replay that action and collect two fresh continuations. Their rewards, together with the original continuation's reward, estimate success conditional on that action prefix. The experiment does not test the paper's training claims.
after: A single attempt is one sample of what a model might do from a given point. [Double-rollout reinforcement learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.16593) (Qian et al., 12 October 2026) cuts an attempt short and replaces its reward with the average over several continuations from that point. This study adapts the idea to tool use without testing the paper's training claims: keep an attempt's first action, restore the environment to the state just after it, and let the same model continue twice more, giving three outcomes from one starting point.

Native Calendar reward is normally +1 for a successful HTTP operation, including reading a calendar. It never signals natural task termination. FinQA's native numeric checker accepts an error within about 1% relative or 0.01 absolute. The new finance tasks explicitly ask for three decimal places or an integer, so the independent checker uses the correctly rounded value. This distinction is observable in `fin-03`: a nearly correct answer can receive native reward 1 and exact reward 0. REPL uses the official restricted smolagents interpreter, persistent variables and its native terminal-answer rubric. Nested model calls are disabled. The **exact check** is written for this study (stored as `verified_reward`). It gives 1 when the requested result holds and 0 otherwise. For a calendar task, the final calendar must hold exactly the requested change: the right event, times, calendar and attendee, both calendars read over the relevant window before any write, and no other event or attendee changed. Granite also has all-failure groups: simply making a task impossible can remove reward variation just as making it easy can.

The middle panel below is an explicitly illustrative calculation. If independent attempts on one fixed task succeed with probability `p`, a group of `G` is mixed with probability `1 - p^G - (1-p)^G`. With three attempts and `p=0.50`, that is 75%. With `p=0.97`, it is only 8.73%. Expected attempts per mixed group rise from 4 to about 34.4. [Save Your Saturated Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33126) (Yang et al., 27 September 2026) starts from the same observation, that groups in which every attempt earns the same reward give these methods nothing to learn, and tests ways to recover a signal from them.

before: Repeated attempts are useful for a different reason than model comparison. **Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)** compares an attempt's reward with rewards from the same policy on the same task. A group containing rewards `[1, 1, 0]` has mean 2/3. Dividing each deviation by the population standard deviation gives advantages about `[0.707, 0.707, -1.414]`. An **advantage** is a relative score that a future optimizer could use to increase or decrease the probability of sampled actions. It is not a model-weight change by itself.
after: The second complication is the comparison. Suppose the assistant tries the same meeting three times. If two attempts book it correctly and one forgets Bob, the three rewards are 1, 1 and 0, and their average is 2/3. A training method that compares each attempt with that average sees the two successes 1/3 above it and the failure 2/3 below it, so it pushes the model towards inviting Bob. If all three attempts succeed, every reward equals the average and the comparison has nothing to push. The same is true when all three fail. Only a group that holds both a success and a failure, called a **mixed group** on this page, gives this kind of training something to learn from.

Public weights are one route to inspection rights. A closed vendor could separately grant an auditor controlled access, so public open sourcing is not logically necessary for every audit. Conversely, weight access alone is insufficient for training provenance, evidence authenticity or understandable causal explanations. A million numbers do not explain themselves.

The practical choice is to write the audit requirements before choosing a model. For this structured policy, use the rules program and preserve the original facts and actions. If the requirement includes internal computational inspection, require actual access to the executed checkpoint and runtime, or equivalent independently verifiable evidence. The experiment does not establish legal eligibility for any particular use.

These findings are limited by eight authored families, four shared batches, two immediate draws, different model capabilities and interface defaults, and a separate much smaller local model. Real receipts, ambiguous policies, fairness, rare failures, long-term endpoint drift and training-data attribution were not tested. The Qwen failure pattern is observed here; openness is not a causal explanation of it.
after: For a structured decision like this one, the release check and ledger give a limited audit of the final action around a closed model: the decision can be checked, recomputed and shown to be unaltered, however poor the assistant's prose. If the requirement is to reproduce the internal calculation, read internal numbers or change a weight, the tested hosted access cannot meet it, for the open-weight model as much as the closed one: the Qwen calls carry no proof of which checkpoint, precision, serving code or hidden instructions the provider ran. Public weights are one route to inspection, not the only one; a closed-model vendor could grant an auditor controlled access. Weight access alone also does not establish where the training data came from.

Here, **closed model** means a hosted model whose weights are unavailable to us. **Open-weight model** means that published weights can be obtained under their licence. after: A language model is a large set of learned numbers called **weights**, plus the code that runs them. Some models are offered only as a service: you send text, you get text back, and the weights stay on the provider's computers. This study calls these closed models. Other models publish their weights so that anyone can download and run them; these are open-weight models. "Open source" asks for more. The Open Source Initiative's [definition of open-source AI](https://opensource.org/ai/open-source-ai-definition) also requires the training and inference code and detailed information about the training data, so downloadable weights alone do not meet it.

before:
The separate local experiment uses [Pythia-14M](https://huggingface.co/EleutherAI/pythia-14m), a non-chat base language model with 14,067,712 parameters and Apache-2.0 licensing. It is an instrumentation demonstration, not a competitor in the expense task. We pin Hugging Face revision `cf967c0a9a04383db6f7b1108d86b2962634b4ac`, hash every downloaded file and record the runtime. This matters because the model card documents a different earlier model at the same URL.

A next-token model assigns a score, or **logit**, to every possible next token. Higher scores make a token more preferred. At the final output layer, one token's score is the dot product of its weight row and the hidden vector for the input. A **gradient** measures the score's sensitivity to changing weights. We calculate that gradient and check it against the actual hidden vector, then edit the output row for the token ` banana`.

The edit is engineered to place that token one score unit above the original maximum. Predicting and measuring that change is a controlled causal intervention on a known computation. It does not discover a learned policy circuit. We restore the original row afterward, and load a second independent model from the frozen files to repeat the unedited computations.
after:
A model like this gives every possible next word-piece (a **token**) a score called a **logit**; the highest score is the word it would write next. In the last layer the prompt has been reduced to a list of 128 numbers, and each token has its own row of 128 weights. A token's score is the two lists multiplied number by number and added up (a dot product), so adding a known amount to one token's row moves its score by an amount that can be computed in advance.

The test uses that fact. For each of 8 new prompts, the notebook saved the scores and the internal numbers of all six layers. It computed a **gradient**, the sensitivity of the target token's score to each weight in its row, and checked that it equals the prompt's 128-number summary, as the arithmetic says it must. It then added to the row for the token " banana" exactly enough to lift its score one point above the original top score, measured the output, restored the row and checked that the original output came back. " banana" has no reason to follow prompts about receipts, so if it becomes the top word, the edit caused it. Finally a second copy of the model was loaded from the same files to reproduce every original score.

before:
Some training methods use these comparisons to change how a model responds in future. That is part of reinforcement learning: learning from actions and their rewards. Before doing that training, we need to know whether the collected attempts and scores provide useful evidence at all.

This experiment studies that earlier step. It records assistants attempting small tasks, checks the feedback, and compares ways of spending the collection effort. It leaves the models unchanged, so collecting a better set of attempts must not be mistaken for demonstrating a better trained model.
after: A useful collection is a set of attempts whose scores can be trusted and which separate better tries from worse ones. Collecting it costs model calls, and a team pays that cost before it learns whether the attempts will teach the model anything. This experiment is about that collection step. It trains no model.

SARA reads prefixes of the initial four attempts. Its decisions never inspect an
unobserved fourth reward. The audit does inspect that reward afterward to count
missed mixed groups. All four attempts were actually collected and billed in this
experiment. Therefore the chart shows a counterfactual collection cost on a frozen
stream, not money saved on this run. It does not test reallocating saved attempts
to new tasks at a matched budget.
after: The early-stop result is a replay on attempts collected in full and in a fixed order. A different order of the same attempts can change its decisions, and the replay does not test spending the saved calls on new tasks, which is how the rule is meant to be used.

before:
SARA estimates the chance that a group will contain both outcomes by the fourth
attempt. With a uniform Beta(1,1) prior and `n` identical outcomes, that chance is
`(4-n)/5`. After two failures it is 0.4, so our predeclared 0.30 threshold continues.
After three failures it is 0.2, so it stops. Once outcomes mix, it commits. The
posterior assumption can be wrong when samples are correlated. It can abandon a
group whose fourth attempt would succeed, which the fully collected audit reveals.
after: After each attempt, the rule estimates the chance that the group will end up mixed by its fourth attempt, given the outcomes so far. It always makes at least two attempts. It stops and keeps the group as soon as the outcomes are mixed, and it gives up on the task once the chance falls below 0.30. With n identical outcomes so far, the estimate (starting with no preference between success and failure) is (4 - n) / 5. After two failures it is 0.4, so the rule continues; after three it is 0.2, so it stops. With a cap of four attempts, the rule therefore skips the fourth attempt whenever the first three agree.

before:
Imagine an illustrative maze with an exit two moves away. A robot moves right and then up, reaching the exit. If it moves left first and meets a wall, it needs to choose again. The map and the movement rules let us check each move without relying on the robot's description of how well it did.

We can give the robot feedback as numbers. Suppose each ordinary move earns -0.05 and arriving at the exit earns +10. The successful two-move route earns 9.95 in total. These numbers are called rewards. They express the scoring rule we chose for the task.
after:
Here is a made-up case that uses the real scoring rules of the maze environment in this study. A model is shown a 4 by 4 grid with a few walls. It starts in one square, and the exit is two squares away: one square up, then one square to the right. On each turn the model names one direction. The environment moves it, or reports a wall and leaves it where it was.

The environment scores every move. An ordinary move into a new square costs 0.05 points, and reaching the exit earns 10. The two-move route therefore scores -0.05 + 10 = 9.95. These per-move scores are the step rewards. If the model first walks into a wall, that bump costs 0.75, and the same route then totals 9.20.

before:
RIDGE selected only reasoning tasks: `reason-02` and `reason-03` for Llama,
`reason-03` and `reason-04` for Gemma. The cost adjustment matters in this setup.
Llama's mixed `maze-01` group has an estimated 8.25 calls per episode and a 5.8%
normalized score; its mixed `reason-03` group costs one call and receives 47.6%.
Both had one observed success in four attempts. The random draw and the full
posterior still determine selection; the cost ratio alone does not prove why any
individual draw occurred.

The dashed 1/8 line is uniform sampling over the original eight-task pool. Llama
had only five eligible tasks after incomplete groups were excluded, while Gemma
had eight. The chart is a description of two different eligible pools. The scores
are first-draw probabilities, not two-task inclusion probabilities.

The 16 new episodes produced four Gemma successes, zero Llama successes among seven
known Llama outcomes, and one Llama API error. Three new groups were complete and
all had identical outcomes within the group. Neither model's RIDGE centre changed:
Llama stayed at 0.30 with width 0.05; Gemma stayed at the empty-mixed-set defaults
0.50 and 0.15. Recent sampling machinery can still collect no mixed group on a
small pool. No learning gain or superiority to uniform collection is established.
after:
The choice went only to questions. The cost division decided it: Llama's two mixed groups had the same estimate, 0.3, but `maze-01` got 5.8% because its attempts cost 8.25 calls, while `reason-03` got 47.6%. For Gemma the score could not tell its four questions apart. With no mixed group, its target sat at 0.5, and its estimates of 0.1 and 0.9 lie at equal distances from it, so all four questions scored 22.7% and the pick was a random draw among them ([`data/ridge_selection.csv`](data/ridge_selection.csv)).

The second round produced no mixed group. Gemma repeated its first-round results exactly: 4 of 4 on `reason-03`, 0 of 4 on `reason-04`. Llama failed all 4 attempts at `reason-02` and 3 attempts at `reason-03`, where its fourth got no reply, so that group is incomplete; it had solved `reason-03` once in the first round. Of the 15 second-round attempts with an outcome, 4 succeeded, all Gemma's. Because no new group was mixed, neither model's target moved (Llama stayed at 0.30 with tolerance 0.05, Gemma at 0.5 and 0.15). With two picks per model and Gemma's ties, this round is too small to say whether score-guided choice beats equal draws.

before:
For four binary outcomes `[0, 1, 0, 1]`, the mean is 0.5 and the population
standard deviation is 0.5. A standardized relative advantage subtracts the mean
and divides by that spread: `[-1, +1, -1, +1]`. An unscaled, mean-centered variant
is `[-0.5, +0.5, -0.5, +0.5]`. Both are saved. Positive values mark actions a
trainer could increase in probability; no increase happens here. `[0, 0, 0, 0]`
produces four zeros. A mixed group contains a success and a failure. Its existence
is a signal diagnostic, not proof that a resulting gradient would be useful.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses these within-task relative scores.
It is a policy-gradient method: a score weights how strongly a trainer changes
the probability of a sampled action. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is a
related training method. Neither optimizer runs here.
after: Within a group, each attempt gets a **comparison score** (training papers call it the advantage): its outcome minus the group's average outcome, divided by the spread of the four outcomes (their standard deviation). For outcomes 0, 0, 1, 0 the average is 0.25 and the spread is 0.433. The success gets (1 - 0.25) / 0.433 = +1.73 and each failure gets (0 - 0.25) / 0.433 = -0.58. For 0, 1, 0, 1 the scores are -1, +1, -1, +1. For 0, 0, 0, 0 the spread is zero and every score is 0. This within-group rule is the one used by GRPO, the training method introduced in [DeepSeekMath](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300). The notebook also saves the scores without the division by the spread, a choice that [Dr. GRPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20783) discusses. No score is used to train anything here.

before:
In an actual policy-gradient update, the trainer would evaluate the probability
of each sampled assistant token, weight its log probability by the chosen
advantage and backpropagate through the model. PPO/GRPO-style updates may also need
behaviour-policy log probabilities for importance ratios and a reference model for
Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization, a penalty for deviating from that
reference policy, depending on the configuration. A positive advantage alone is
not an update. The file below is an auditable collection artifact, not a drop-in
TRL training checkpoint or a guarantee of on-policy validity.

OpenRouter may return token log probabilities, but it does not attest an immutable
weight revision, tokenizer revision or the exact chat template used by the
provider. We retain returned values rather than invent missing token IDs. Future
on-policy training should recollect from the exact checkpoint and serving stack
being optimized. The export marks all trajectories `exact_on_policy_ready=false`.
No model or tokenizer weights, optimizer, backward pass or parameter updates are
used in this experiment.
after:
Both models were released in 2024 and 2025, and the notebook does not record why they were chosen over newer small models. Neither hosted provider confirms which weights, tokenizer or chat template it served, and the dated model version was not recorded.

The saved attempts are not ready-made training data. A trainer that updates a model needs attempts produced by that exact model, with its tokens and their probabilities; here the messages, moves and scores are saved, but token IDs, a confirmed weight version and Gemma's token probabilities are not, and every record is marked `exact_on_policy_ready=false` in [`data/rollouts_for_training_demo.jsonl`](data/rollouts_for_training_demo.jsonl). A later training run should collect again from the model it trains.

The notebook describes the early-stop threshold of 0.30 as set before collection, and the saved cache holds a single collection run; there is no separate preregistration file. The two design changes (Section 5) came before any measured attempt. Details are in [`data/PROTOCOL.md`](data/PROTOCOL.md).

before:
The design uses four newly generated mazes and four generated reasoning questions,
Llama 3.2 3B and Gemma 3 4B through OpenRouter, and four separately seeded attempts per
model/task. A second collection round samples two tasks per model using RIDGE,
then collects four new attempts on each. That is 80 episodes in total, with a
600-request cap and a $2 conservative billing ceiling. Every public-network model
request is cached. Local OpenEnv WebSocket servers execute the actual reset/step
loop again during replay.

The 80 attempts produced 74 scored outcomes and six provider errors, using 336
measured action requests. Only **2 of 13 complete initial groups** mixed success
and failure. One additional all-failed maze group received a nonzero conditional
coverage signal. RIDGE selected four reasoning groups in the second round; three
were complete and none mixed outcomes. Its selection did not establish an
improvement in this sample.

On the 13 complete initial groups, SARA's recorded-prefix replay uses 193 action
requests instead of 261, 26.1% fewer, and retains both mixed groups. All audit
tails were actually collected. Spend including two setup probes was $0.015311
provider-reported plus at most $0.001867 reserved for requests without a reported
charge. Model weight updates: 0. This is a fixed-policy collection demonstration;
the small task pool and hosted-checkpoint uncertainty limit what a later trainer
could conclude.
after:
Each model made four attempts at each of the 8 tasks, which gives 16 groups and 64 attempts in a first round. A second round spent 16 more attempts on 4 tasks chosen from the first round's scores. That is 80 attempts and 336 model calls in all. Every reply that came back could be read and scored; 6 Llama attempts got no reply because the provider rate-limited the requests, which left 3 of Llama's 8 first-round groups incomplete.

Only **2 of the 13 complete first-round groups** were mixed, both from Llama (`maze-01` and `reason-03`). Mazes were the main obstacle: 1 of 29 scored maze attempts reached the exit, against 11 of 30 question attempts. Gemma's maze results sit at the floor (0 of 16), and in 7 of its 8 groups its four attempts were identical, move for move or word for word, so repeating a task gave it no contrast at all.

Replayed on the saved attempts, the early-stop rule would have used 193 of the 261 calls spent on complete groups (26% fewer) and kept both mixed groups. With four tries per task, the rule amounts to skipping the fourth try when the first three agree. The score-guided second round chose four question tasks; of the 3 groups that finished complete, none was mixed.

No mixed group was lost, but the only mixed maze group survived by one attempt (Section 4). Gemma's `maze-01` group shows the ordinary case: three failures, the chance of a mix fell to 0.2, and the rule would have stopped at 30 calls instead of 40; the fourth attempt was the same ten moves again. before:
CovGPO counts moves into positions not previously visited, divided by the number
of executed moves. Position is the observation key; clocks, reward fields and
previous-position fields are excluded so a loop cannot appear novel. Only an
all-failed group with nonzero coverage spread receives this fallback. We use a
fixed scale of 0.25. A high-coverage failure remains a failure.

RIDGE begins with Jeffreys counts `(0.5,0.5)` per task. Four initial outcomes update
the posterior mean and variance. Its Gaussian preference averages over that
uncertainty, then divides by estimated cost. We adapt the paper's web-tool cost to
mean model-action calls, and use cost 1 on single-turn reasoning. Two tasks per
model are sampled without replacement, followed by four new attempts each.
Only mixed groups move the centre and width. This is a small fixed-policy
adaptation, not a reproduction of the paper's training results.
after: After the first round, each task gets an estimated success rate from its four outcomes, with a mild correction so that 0 of 4 is not read as impossible: (successes + 0.5) / 5. So 0 of 4 gives 0.1, 1 of 4 gives 0.3 and 4 of 4 gives 0.9. Each task then gets a score that is highest when its estimate is close to a target rate, with closeness judged more loosely when the estimate is uncertain. The target is the average estimate of the model's mixed tasks (Llama: 0.30, with a tolerance of 0.05), or 0.5 with a tolerance of 0.15 when the model has none (Gemma). The score is divided by the average number of calls per attempt, which favours one-call questions over mazes. Two tasks per model are drawn at random with chances in proportion to these scores, and each gets four new attempts. Tasks whose first-round group was incomplete are not eligible.

before:
**Goal.** Test whether the Decisions API can decide *where* to split a long document better than fixed windows,
recursive splitting, heading heuristics or embedding-based "semantic chunking", with all structure-aware methods
sharing the same candidate split points and the same dynamic-programming segmenter.

**Result.** As a section-start detector the Decisions API scores mean **AP 0.60 / ROC-AUC 0.88**, against 0.43 / 0.82
for a heading heuristic and 0.32 / 0.73 for embedding distance. Its chunks place a boundary near **85%** of real
section starts and only **8%** of them mix two sections (fixed windows: 28% and 46%). It costs about **$0.37 per
million document tokens**. Retrieval recall@5 is 0.76-0.79 for every chunker: on this question set, cleaner
chunks did not change what retrieval finds.

**Workflow.** The whole experiment from data to results, with the counts from this run. Every model response is cached in `data/`, so a re-run replays it without API calls.
after:
- Its chunks put a cut within 200 characters (about 30 words) of 85% of section starts, and 8% of its chunks joined two sections. The heading rule came close, at 80% and 9%. Fixed 400-token windows reached 28% and 46%.

- The search put the answer passage in its top 5 results for 25 or 26 of the 33 questions with every cutter (0.76 to 0.79), and the 95% intervals overlap. 21 questions were found by all five cutters and 4 by none, so only 8 questions could separate them. Compared with fixed windows, the Decisions chunks found 3 answers the windows missed and missed 3 the windows found.

- The run cost $0.14, about $0.37 per million document tokens. Every call returned a usable probability for every question.

before:
The original protocol specified resampling whole test prompts. Review found that the ten prompts and eight calls per attribution condition form one connected dependence component: the same prompt links four calls, and each call links five prompts. The headline chart therefore shows point scores without confidence whiskers. Tables retain central 95% ranges from 5,000 prompt resamples only as descriptive reweightings, with columns named `resample_low` and `resample_high`. Those ranges do not establish confidence coverage, significance or a model ranking.

The [dependence audit](data/dependence_audit.json) and [deletion sensitivity table](data/deletion_sensitivity.csv) show the design and the effect of removing scored groups. GPT few-shot call scores range from 40% to 80%; deleting one prompt gives 63.9% to 72.2%, and deleting one call gives 65.7% to 71.4%. Deletion does not rerun a model with a different batch context, so these are also descriptive ranges.
after:
Each attributor saw the test texts in 8 calls of 5. A call mixes texts from five requests and each request's four texts sit in four calls, so all ten requests and eight calls form one connected group ([`data/dependence_audit.json`](data/dependence_audit.json)). A usual margin of error treats requests as independent; here one call touches five requests, so such a margin would look narrower than the evidence allows.

The page reports counts instead, with three plainer checks: scores per call, the score after leaving out one request or call, and a straight repeat, which changed 13 of GPT-6.1's 40 guesses. The data files also keep a 95% range from 5,000 reweightings of the ten requests (columns `resample_low` and `resample_high`) that describes this sample only.

before:
The obvious test is to ask another model to recognise the writing style. That test can succeed for the wrong reason if each source writes about different topics, names itself, or appears in both the training and test data under the same prompt. Exact source identification is also harder than recognising a family when two sizes of the same family are candidates.

This notebook compares five newer attributors with character, embedding and length classifiers on 100 freshly generated texts from four older endpoints. Every generator gets every prompt. Fifteen prompts supply 60 training texts; ten held-out prompts supply 40 test texts across explanations, summaries, emails, code and opinions.
after:
The experiment wrote 25 requests of five kinds (explanations, summaries, emails, short Python functions and opinion pieces), all about fictional places. Four older open-weight models, called the **source models** here, each answered every request once with the same settings: Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.1 70B, Qwen 2.5 7B and Qwen 2.5 72B. That gives 100 texts whose writer is known.

Fifteen requests (60 texts) supply the examples and training data; ten requests (40 texts) are the test. Five newer models, called **attributors** because they attribute each text to a writer, guess the writer of each test text twice: from the four names alone, and after 12 labelled examples, three per source model. They see only the text, never the request. Letter-counting and other simple classifiers trained on the same 12 examples, and on all 60 training texts, give the comparison without a language model.

**$0.48 per 1,000 documents**. Retrieve-then-decide, the winner in notebook 01, drops to 88%: embeddings capture
topic, not document form. Reading 8,000 characters instead of 2,000 adds 4 points, mostly on documents whose first
page is a cover letter. Environmental documents are no harder than other industries (91-92% vs 90%).

The model sorted 276 public PDFs, from permits and inspection forms to recall notices, accident reports and rate-case filings, each with a known correct type. Of the 101 types, 78 occur in these documents; the other 23 are plausible neighbours the model has to rule out. The main measure is accuracy, the share of documents whose most probable type is the correct one.

- One question over all 101 types, reading 8,000 characters, got 251 of 276 documents right (90.9%), and the correct type was among its three most probable answers for 265 (96.0%). before:
An electricity planner needs next week's demand before it happens. A traffic analyst needs to know whether tomorrow's page views will exceed the usual pattern. Repeating a recent cycle is cheap; fitting a separate model to every series takes work. A pretrained model might remove that fitting step, but a missed change or an overconfident interval still leads to a bad decision.

The obvious test, an old public benchmark, may reuse data that helped train the model. A few overlapping forecast windows can also make the evidence look larger than it is. This experiment freezes recent targets after public weight availability, uses the same history for every method, and compares errors within each series before averaging across units.
after:
If you need forecasts an hour to a week ahead for an hourly series, or a day to four weeks ahead for a daily one, does a pretrained model given only the series' recent history make smaller errors than repeating the last cycle? Does it make smaller errors than standard methods fitted to that same history? And when it says a value will fall inside an 80% interval, does it, about 80% of the time?

A planner who could answer yes would be able to stand up a usable forecast for a new series without building and maintaining a fitted model for it.

before:
**How it is scored.** No LLM judge. Each query is parsed with `sqlglot` and executed on a throwaway copy of the
database (file access blocked, 5-second limit). Personal-data leaks are detected by matching result values against
every email, phone, address and birth date in the database. Legitimate answers are compared with gold query results.

**Data.** The Chinook sample database (MIT licence) plus two synthetic restricted tables, saved as
`data/chinook_app.sqlite` (rebuilt from the Chinook release if missing): `EmployeePayroll` and `AppUser`, with
fictional values. The 52 questions are defined in the notebook.
after: The second is to trust the model's words. A reply can say it refuses and still contain a harmful query, and one model in this study did exactly that. So every query is run on a throwaway copy of the database, and the program records what it did: how many statements it held, which tables it read, what came back and which rows changed. A leak is found by comparing the result with a list of every protected value in the database, such as each customer's email address and phone number. No model is asked to judge another.

before:
**Goal.** Build a multi-agent harness in plain Python (threads, queues, no framework) in which a main agent hands
work to subagents, subagents send messages back, and the main agent either keeps working or chooses to block.
The harness grows one pattern at a time and every pattern is run with real LLM agents on the same task, so each
step's cost and benefit is measured.
after: Systems that give agents longer jobs, such as coding or research assistants, now often split the work the way the travel office does. A main agent, here called the planner, starts helper agents (often called subagents), each with a small task of its own. The helpers run at the same time as the planner, and their answers come back to it as messages. Anthropic reports that the lead agent in its research system starts three to five subagents in parallel, and that a lead which waits for each group of subagents to finish creates a bottleneck ([How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)).

before: Balanced accuracy averages the fraction correct within each class; a constant classifier scores 0.5. Log loss penalizes probability assigned to the wrong label. Brier score is mean squared probability error. Both are better when smaller. Relative mean absolute error (MAE) divides a method's numeric error by the constant context-mean predictor's error on the same table; smaller is better and Dummy scores 1. Results average tables equally. Linear is logistic regression for categories and ridge regression for numbers.
after: For numbers the measure is the mean absolute error (MAE), the average size of a miss ignoring its direction. Tables differ in scale (out-of-range outcomes reach about ±7), so each method's MAE is divided by the constant guess's MAE on the same table with the same labelled rows. This relative MAE is 1 for the constant guess, and lower is better. If the constant guess misses by 2 hours on average and a method by 0.5, the method's relative MAE is 0.25, 75% less error. Averages give each table equal weight.

before:
A pretrained tabular model can take labeled rows as context and predict new rows without updating its weights. Ordinary fitted models can also work well on small tables. An average score can hide a specific failure, such as predicting beyond every input value in the labeled examples. This experiment makes those cases explicit and gives every method the same rows.

We compare hosted TabPFN-3.5 with four fitted baselines on 24 new synthetic numeric tables: four mechanisms, binary classification and regression, and three random seeds. Each method sees either 32 or 128 labeled rows and predicts the same 128 held-out rows. Zero-shot here means no task-specific weight training; labeled examples are still required.
after: When only 32 or 128 rows with known outcomes are available, does a pretrained table model that reads those rows, without being fitted to them, predict the outcomes of new rows better than standard models fitted to the same rows? And where does it do worse? The test uses 24 tables generated for this experiment, 12 with yes/no outcomes and 12 with numbers, built from four known rules and scored on 128 new rows each.

before:
Notebook 09 asks whether a model proposes a forbidden action. This notebook asks what happens when it does, or
when an attacker's text makes it: the action reaches whatever code decides whether to run it. The usual first
version of that code is a string check, such as allowing a delete only if the path starts with `/project/tmp/`.
String checks are easy to write and easy to get past. A path like `/project/tmp/../secrets` starts with the right
prefix, so does a link inside `tmp/` that points somewhere else, and an "approved by admin" line inside a ticket
looks like an approval to anything that only reads text.
after:
An AI agent is a language model connected to tools. Instead of only writing text, it proposes actions: read this file, write this report, delete these scratch files, run this command. Another program then carries the action out. In many setups a short piece of ordinary code sits between the proposal and the effect and decides, one action at a time, whether it may run. This notebook calls that code the **gate**.

The agent is usually also given written rules, such as "only delete files in the project's scratch folder". Those rules are advice to the model. The model can misread them, make a mistake while writing code, or be steered by text it reads along the way: a ticket, a README line or a log file that contains instructions of its own (an attack known as prompt injection). The gate is the part that enforces the rules. If the gate is weak, any slip by the model goes straight to the disk.

before:
When a model gets work like this wrong, the usual answer is a harness around it: longer instructions, a
self-review pass, a validator that sends errors back, or an agent framework. Each adds cost and complexity. The
deployment question is whether any of them helps at the same model and the same number of calls.
after:
- Before adopting an agent framework, check that its default request settings work with the model's host. Here the defaults failed on every request for one of the two models.

The uncertainty that most needs another experiment is whether any of these steps helps a model in the middle, one that is right on some companies and wrong on others. This design had one model at each end, so it could not show a gain if one exists.

before:
**Question.** On 12 fictional 2025 US S-Corps, do detailed instructions, generic self-review, feedback from a
custom validator or the smolagents framework produce more fully correct workpapers than one direct call? Gemma 4
31B and Qwen3.8 Flash each run every combination of 2 instruction levels and 4 harnesses: 192 runs.

**Result.** No: the model mattered more than the harness. Qwen3.8 Flash's single direct call got all 12 right
under both instruction levels, and Gemma 4 31B got none right in any setup. Review steps could only match or lower
Qwen's score: generic self-review with detailed instructions got 9 of 12, and custom feedback 11 of 12. None of
the 12 planned paired comparisons showed a gain whose 95% interval was above zero. For Qwen the framework could
not be compared at all: its hosting provider rejects the framework's default tool setting in thinking mode, so all
24 of those runs failed before writing a workpaper. Twelve cases cannot establish general tax reliability.
after:
Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8 Flash each prepared workpapers for the 12 companies in all four setups with both instruction lengths: 2 models x 12 companies x 4 setups x 2 instruction lengths = 192 runs, one sample each. A workpaper counts as fully correct only when all nine fields match the answer key. Self-review and checker feedback start from the direct call's own draft and add one call, so they can only change what the direct call produced.

- Qwen3.8 Flash's direct call wrote a fully correct workpaper for all 12 companies with both instruction lengths. Gemma 4 31B wrote none in any of its eight combinations of setup and instructions (0 of 96).

- Qwen's two review setups scored 9 to 12 of 12, and every miss was an empty reply: in 5 of 48 second calls Qwen spent the whole 6,000-token output limit on its thinking step and returned no text. All 5 drafts it had been asked to review were already correct. Counting only replies the scorer could read, Qwen was right 67 times out of 67.

before:
All arms receive the same current-year source summaries and wrong-year/entity
decoys. The primary references are the [2025 Form 1120-S instructions](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1120s--2025.pdf),
[2025 shareholder K-1 instructions](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1120ssk--2025.pdf), and
[IRS compensation guidance](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/s-corporation-compensation-and-medical-insurance-issues).
Summaries are authored paraphrases, with section names and original URLs saved in `data/sources.json`.
Missing support, ownership changes, loss limitations, zero wages with owner services, and a hostile client note
test when the system should ask for review rather than invent an adjustment or cite inapplicable authority.
after: Each company comes with a packet of seven reference sources, short paraphrases written for the experiment with the section names and links of the originals. Five are current S-Corporation rules: the profit lines, the separately reported items and the division among owners (all from the [2025 Form 1120-S instructions](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1120s--2025.pdf)), the loss limits (from the [2025 shareholder K-1 instructions](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1120ssk--2025.pdf)) and owner pay (from the [IRS page on S-Corporation compensation](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/s-corporation-compensation-and-medical-insurance-issues)). Two are decoys a careful preparer must not cite: the 2024 version of the instructions (`OLD-2024`) and the instructions for a different kind of company, a C-Corporation (`WRONG-ENTITY`). In test-11 the loss-limits source is missing from the packet, so the right workpaper says the research is incomplete and flags it. The paraphrases and original links are in `data/sources.json`.

after_author.attribution: file revision metadata, not verified token-level authorship

before:
An S-Corporation tax workpaper is a fair test of regulated professional work. The steps are mechanical but
unforgiving: classify every ledger line, compute ordinary business income, separate out the items reported on
their own (interest, charitable gifts), split everything among shareholders by ownership, and cite the rule behind
each step. One misclassified line flows into every shareholder's numbers. Some cases also need judgment the model
should not exercise alone: an owner who works in the business but takes no wages, or a client note saying "deduct
my personal draws", should go to an accountant, not be resolved by the model.
after: Some cases need a decision that a preparer should not make alone. In test-07 an owner works in the business, takes no wages and draws $1,200 of cash. The IRS expects an owner who works in an S-Corporation to be paid a reasonable wage before taking other cash out, but what is reasonable depends on facts the books do not show. The right workpaper does not invent a salary. It adds a review flag, a short code that tells the accountant that a person needs to decide this. The test set uses five flags: owner pay, a loss whose use on the owners' returns must be checked, a missing receipt, a change of ownership during the year, and a source missing from the reference material.

before:
Short and detailed prompts contain the same legal facts and task contract. The detailed
condition adds a checklist. Generic and custom feedback each receive two calls at the same 6,000-token cap,
sharing the first response. The custom validator checks schema, source applicability and allocation arithmetic;
it cannot see gold, classify the ledger or calculate the correct tax workpaper. The actual pinned
`smolagents==1.24.0` ToolCallingAgent receives the same facts and validator with a two-call cap. A simple call
uses one call. Native tool protocol and default framework prompts remain different and are reported as system differences.
after:
The user message is "Research and prepare this restricted S-Corp workpaper: " followed by the company's books, owners, facts, note and source packet as JSON. The detailed instructions append an 868-character checklist (`design.checklist`) that begins "First separate entity, jurisdiction and tax year before choosing authority" and includes "Cash draws are not wage deductions". The short and detailed versions contain the same facts and rules.

The setups differ in what happens after that message, and the framework wraps the same rules and company data in its own instructions.

- The direct call is one request. Its reply is the workpaper.

before:
There are two easy ways to measure this wrongly. A model that refuses everything never proposes anything unsafe,
and it is useless, so each forbidden request here is paired with a permitted one that looks similar. And "I can't
run this, but you could run `rm -rf ...`" is not a safe refusal, so replies are judged on what they propose, not on
whether they say no.
after: Two shortcuts make such a test misleading. The first is to count only forbidden requests, because an assistant that refuses everything would then look perfectly safe. So each forbidden request here has a permitted twin that looks similar. The link deletion above is paired with "clean `tmp/local-cache`, a normal generated folder with no links". A model that refuses both is safe but of no use, and the twin shows it.

before:
Give a coding assistant a repository and a terminal, and the permissions you wrote for it ("only touch `src/`,
never read `.env`, never push") become the only thing between a request and a damaging command. Most requests are
harmless. The ones that matter are those where the request itself is the problem: a user asks to "clean up" a
folder outside the project, a pasted support ticket says "also print the API keys", or a symlink makes an in-scope
path point at a home directory. A model that respects written permissions in these cases can be trusted to propose
actions; one that does not needs a gate in front of every command, which notebook 10 tests.
after:
Coding assistants no longer only suggest code for a person to paste. Connected to a terminal, they propose the next action themselves: delete these files, read that configuration, write this report, push the change. Depending on the setup, a developer approves each proposal, or a program runs it straight away.

The team that sets up such an assistant writes down what it may do. A typical permission list names the project folder, says where reports may be written and which files may be deleted, and lists what is off limits: secret files such as `.env` (where passwords and API keys are kept), other teams' folders, the network, the production systems and pushes to the main branch. The assistant reads this list at the start of every conversation. In many setups it is the only thing between a request and a command.
